reference: Apply a tourniquet 5 to 7 centimetres above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until bleeding stops. Write the time on the skin. Do not remove it in the field. Lay them down, keep them warm and still, and watch for shock.

Press a clean cloth or folded pad firmly onto the wound with the heel of your hand. Do not lift it to check. If it soaks through, add another on top. Maintain pressure at least 10 minutes. Raise the limb unless a fracture is suspected. If bleeding continues, apply a tourniquet.

Lifting a soaked dressing tears off the forming clot, and clotting is how bleeding stops, so the wound rebleeds and restarts from zero. It also introduces contamination. Add a second dressing on top and maintain firm pressure. Do not remove a dressing once applied.

Clean with soap and water. Sterilise fine-pointed tweezers with alcohol or a flame and let them cool. Grip the splinter close to the skin and pull it out at the angle it entered. Do not dig, squeeze or break it. Clean again and cover with a dressing. Seek care if deep, broken below the surface, or infected.

Do not remove the object; removing it can cause sudden heavy bleeding. Build padding around it on both sides, then bandage over the padding without pressing deeper. Do not press on the object. Immobilise the area. Lay them down, keep them still and warm, and watch for shock.

Suspect internal bleeding if the abdomen is tender, rigid or distended; there is bruising over the abdomen, flanks or groin; the person coughs or vomits blood or passes blood in urine; or shock develops with no visible wound. Lay them flat, raise the legs unless spinal or leg injury is suspected, keep them still and warm. Give nothing to eat or drink. Evacuate fast.

Movement raises heart rate and blood pressure, which can dislodge a forming clot. Cold constricts peripheral vessels, diverts blood from vital organs, and impairs clotting directly. Stillness protects the clot and lowers demand on a compromised circulation; warmth keeps clotting working. Together they slow hypovolaemic shock.

Start CPR now. Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, the other interlocked on top. Compress at least 5 centimetres at 100 to 120 per minute with full recoil. Give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions if willing and able; otherwise compress continuously. Send anyone present for an AED. Continue until signs of life or help arrives.

Check the scene is safe. Tap the shoulders and shout. If no response, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasping is not normal breathing. If breathing is not normal, start CPR. Do not delay CPR to check a pulse.

Effective compressions depress the chest at least 5 centimetres with full recoil each time; keep hands in contact but release pressure completely between compressions. Rate 100 to 120 per minute, about two per second. Depth falls as the rescuer tires, so swap every two minutes if possible. Keep interruptions under 10 seconds.

Turn the AED on and follow its prompts. Place pads on bare dry skin, one below the right collarbone, one on the left chest below the armpit. Ensure nobody touches the person during analysis. If a shock is advised, warn everyone, confirm no contact, then shock. Resume compressions immediately.

Stopping compressions drops coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure to zero immediately, and it takes several seconds to rebuild it. Frequent pauses therefore cut resuscitation effectiveness. Pulse checks are also unreliable: rescuers and clinicians alike misjudge them under stress. The cost of the pause is certain; the value of the check is not.

Start CPR immediately: 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, at least 5 centimetres deep, 100 to 120 per minute. With no way to call for help, stay and keep compressing; leaving the patient more than 10 seconds sharply reduces survival. For a child, give 2 minutes of CPR before briefly leaving to signal.

Give nothing to eat or drink. Do not induce vomiting. Note the time swallowed and the object type. A button battery in the oesophagus burns tissue within 2 hours; magnets attract through bowel walls and can perforate. Both need urgent endoscopy. Get the child to a facility capable of emergency endoscopy fast.

Do not rub the eye. Tilt the head with the affected eye down and pour clean water or saline from the inner corner outward to flush it out. If visible on the white of the eye, lift it away with the damp corner of a clean cloth. If flushing fails or pain persists, cover the eye without pressure and seek care.

Rubbing drives a surface particle deeper into the conjunctiva or cornea, turning a loose object into an embedded one, and abrades the cornea, which is painful and infection-prone. A metal fragment can be pushed through the globe, risking permanent vision loss. Flush gently with water instead.

Transport urgently for: temperature above 40 degrees Celsius; any fever above 38 degrees in an infant under 3 months; a rash that does not fade under pressure, suggesting meningococcal disease; seizure with fever; difficulty waking; difficulty breathing; a very unwell appearance; stiff neck or bulging fontanelle.

Check for a response. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. If breathing, lay them flat and raise the legs above heart level. Loosen tight clothing. Give nothing to eat or drink. Do not leave them alone. Once conscious, keep them lying down before letting them sit up slowly.

Treat it as an emergency. Tilt the head back and lift the chin. If breathing, roll them onto their side into the recovery position and monitor breathing. If breathing stops, start CPR. Note the time of collapse. Do not leave them alone. Evacuate urgently.

Do not straighten the arm. Support it in the position found. Make a sling from a triangular bandage or improvised cloth to hold the arm across the chest at about 90 degrees of elbow flexion. Pad bony prominences. Never bandage over the fracture site. Check circulation, sensation and movement in the fingers before and after.

Fracture is more likely with an audible crack or snap; visible deformity or abnormal angulation; crepitus on palpation; severe pain worsening with pressure over the bone; swelling and bruising within minutes; inability to bear weight; numbness or tingling below the injury; or bone visible through the skin. If in doubt, treat as a fracture: immobilise and keep weight off.

Sharp bone ends can lacerate arteries, veins and nerves, and forcing the limb can tent the skin and convert a closed fracture to an open one. Forcing a dislocation can trap bone or soft tissue in the joint and permanently compromise its blood supply. Immobilise in the position found, padded. Do not reduce or realign.

RICE is Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Rest: stop activity. Ice: a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes every 2 hours for 48 hours, never directly on skin. Compression: a firm elastic bandage, checking circulation to fingers or toes. Elevation: raise the limb above heart level. Not for fractures, dislocations or open wounds.

Stop the activity and have the person sit or lie down. Stretch the calf by pulling the toes and ball of the foot toward the shin, holding steadily without forcing. Do not massage hard during the cramp. If the calf is swollen and tender, seek assessment for deep vein thrombosis.

Lower them to the ground. Do not restrain them. Do not put anything in their mouth. Clear hard objects away and put something soft under the head. Note the time it starts. When convulsions stop, roll them onto their side into the recovery position and monitor breathing. Seek assessment for a first seizure, one over 5 minutes, or failure to return to normal awareness.

After a concussion the brain has reduced blood flow and impaired energy regulation. Exertion raises metabolic demand exactly when the brain cannot meet it, prolonging symptoms. A second impact before the first resolves can cause second-impact syndrome, a rapid and potentially fatal brain swelling. Resume only through a graduated protocol after a symptom-free period.

Hypoglycaemia develops over minutes: pale sweaty skin, shakiness, confusion, hunger, palpitations, glucose below 4 mmol/L. Hyperglycaemia develops over hours: heavy thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, fatigue. If unsure and the person is conscious and can swallow safely, give sugar. If they cannot swallow safely, give nothing by mouth. Seek care if no improvement within 15 minutes.

Warning signs include sudden lightheadedness, pale or ashen skin, cold clammy sweating, nausea, tunnel vision or greying out, a slow weak pulse, ringing in the ears, and leg weakness. These appear 30 seconds to a few minutes before collapse. Get them lying flat and raise their legs.

Lean the person forward and give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking the mouth after each. If they fail, give up to 5 chest thrusts: same landmark as CPR compressions, on the lower half of the breastbone, but sharper and slower. Alternate until it clears. If they lose consciousness, start CPR.

Keep them calm and upright, leaning slightly forward. Do not lay them flat. Give 4 puffs of the blue reliever every 4 minutes while preparing for evacuation. Do not give sedatives or antihistamines. No response after 4 or more puffs means a life-threatening attack needing hospital treatment. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.

An unconscious person loses the reflexes that stop the tongue obstructing the airway and stop vomit being inhaled. Lying on the side with the top knee bent forward and the head tilted back keeps the airway open and lets fluid drain. Do not use it if spinal injury is suspected unless the airway cannot be maintained otherwise.

Start CPR if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally after removal from the water. Agonal gasping is not normal breathing. Coughing, spluttering or movement means they are breathing: monitor closely, as deterioration can be delayed. Anyone rescued needs medical assessment even if apparently recovered. For drowning, give 5 rescue breaths before compressions.

Apply pressure immobilisation immediately. Do not wash the bite: residual venom identifies the species and determines the antivenom. Starting at the toes, wrap a firm elastic or crepe bandage upward over the whole limb, as firmly as for a sprain. Add a second bandage as far up the limb as possible and splint with rigid material. The person must not walk. Evacuate urgently for antivenom; the bandage stays on until hospital.

Flood the sting with undiluted vinegar immediately for at least 30 seconds. Do not rub the area, apply fresh water, or handle tentacles bare-handed; each triggers further venom release. Remove tentacles with tweezers or gloved hands after the vinegar. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR at once.

Cutting and sucking remove negligible venom while causing tissue damage and infection risk. Washing removes the residual venom used to identify the species, which determines the antivenom given. A tourniquet causes ischaemic damage while doing nothing to stop spread, because Australian snake venom travels via the lymphatic system. Pressure immobilisation is the only evidence-based first aid.

Heat stroke is life-threatening. Recognise it by core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius, hot dry skin, confusion or unconsciousness, and a rapid strong pulse. Move to the coolest place and remove excess clothing. Cool at once: ice packs to neck, armpits and groin; wet the skin and fan vigorously; or immerse in cool water if safe. Give no fluids to anyone confused or unconscious. Begin cooling within minutes.

Cool the burn under cool running water for a full 20 minutes immediately. Do not use ice, iced water, butter, toothpaste or creams. Then cover loosely with clean non-fluffy material such as cling film. Do not wrap tightly or burst blisters. Remove rings and tight clothing before swelling begins, unless stuck to the wound. Seek hospital assessment.

Butter, oils and toothpaste trap heat in burned tissue and block the cooling running water provides. They also feed bacteria, raising infection risk. Ice constricts vessels at the burn margins, reducing blood flow to tissue that might survive, and risks frostbite. Cool running water for 20 minutes is the only evidence-based treatment.

Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion and fatigue, resembling flu without fever. Several people or pets affected in the same space suggests it. Do not enter without breathing apparatus. Move the person to fresh air if safe. Monitor breathing, as effects can worsen after apparent recovery. If unresponsive, start CPR.

Do not induce vomiting. Note any medication containers. Keep the person awake and talking. If they become drowsy, roll them onto their side into the recovery position. Give nothing to eat or drink. Monitor breathing. If breathing stops or becomes abnormal, start CPR. Transport urgently with all containers.

Do not move a suspected spinal injury casualty unless there is immediate danger to life. If movement is unavoidable, one person holds the head in neutral alignment with the spine. Use a log-roll with a minimum of three rescuers: one controls the head, two roll the body as one rigid unit. Do not sit or stand the casualty.
